Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

ability noun

the power to do something

also abilities, capability, to the best of my ability

classical

Quint. 10.1.11: loquendī facultāte caruērunt
Traupman 28, 149, 267

facultās, facultātis f.

noun, third declension

ability, capacity; the means or chance to do something

With a gerund in the genitive for what one can do: dīcendī facultās, the ability to speak; legendī scrībendīque facultās, the ability to read and write (Traupman 267). To the best of my ability, prō meā parte (Traupman 92, 267), or Livy’s prō virīlī parte (praef. 3).

Other words

  • potestās, potestātis f. — the power or possibility of doing something

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short s.v. potestās: “ability, power of doing any thing (class.)”

    More often the power one is given, or an opportunity, than an ability one has.

Examples

  • īnfantēs ā mūtīs nūtrīcibus jussū rēgum in sōlitūdine ēducātī, etiamsī verba quaedam ēmīsisse trāduntur, tamen loquendī facultāte caruērunt

    babies brought up in solitude by mute nurses on the orders of kings, though they are said to have uttered some words, still lacked the ability to speakQuint. 10.1.11

  • neque longiōra mihi darī spatia vīvendī volō quam dum erō ad hanc quoque facultātem scrībendī commentandīque idōneus

    and I want no longer span of life than while I am still able to write and take notesGell. praef. 24

  • juvābit tamen rērum gestārum memoriae prīncipis terrārum populī prō virīlī parte et ipsum cōnsuluisse

    still, it will be a pleasure to have done, to the best of my ability, my own part for the memory of the deeds of the foremost people on earthLiv. praef. 3

See also able, ability, skill.

SourcesLewis & Short: facultas · Lewis & Short: potestas
